It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing a world that seeks to “remodel the way we think about truth” by measuring human worth through a "string of degrees" or the "homes they own," and I must ask you with a gentle heart: why do you ask after the spiritual danger of economic indicators and the divergence of markets in this hour? [879, 1348, 1405, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” by the “noise and tumult” of financial precarity, or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that the Master “sovereignly orders everything He has made”—including the rise and fall of "most formidable" economies? [13, 20, 21, 1143, 1408, 1532, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to offer “spiritual placebos” like the "prosperity gospel"—which suggests that "human success" is always "divine blessing"—we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs the “vicissitudes of life” [1, 11, 28, 550, 1503, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, the "administrative anomaly" of economic divergence is subject to the “decree from God” who “works all things according to the counsel of His own will” (Ephesians 1:11) [15, 68, 395, 405, 1143, 1532, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The Spiritual Peril of Material Measurement**

**Verse**
“ ‘And He said to them, “Take heed and beware of covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” ’ ” (Luke 12:15). [298, 1222, 1341, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The sources teach that “unbelief is the seed” of the opinion that human flourishing is found in "material prosperity," for “the carnal mind is enmity against God” (Romans 8:7) [1326, 1412, 1500, Conversation History]. Those who teach that we can “demand things of God” for self-indulgence are “spiritual swindlers” whose “idea of righteousness was mostly cosmetic,” for “you cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24) [6, 187, 430, 520, 556, 702, 1520, Conversation History]. To measure a man by his "brand identity" or "numerical growth" is a "spirit of fraud" that ignores the "standard of absolute holiness" (Hebrews 12:14) [1121, 1233, 1307, 1351, 1512, 1556, 1566, Conversation History]. Measuring flourishing by the "lust of the eyes" and the "pride of life" leads to a "tragic train of thought" where the soul is "past feeling" (1 John 2:16; Ephesians 4:19) [132, 133, 893, 1053, 1184, 1606, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not be deceived” by a “worldly philosophy” that suggests financial "stability" is the same as "salvation," for "the form of this world is passing away" (1 Corinthians 7:31) [91, 286, 314, 1421, 1432, 1434, 1502, 1617, 1684, Conversation History]. "Trade in your worry for trust," recognizing that your "sole objective" is to find the "repose of the soul" in Christ, for “the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17) [24, 36, 101, 172, 220, 1154, 1406, 1408, 1515, 1670, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **Jewish context**, "national greatness" and "large and beautiful cities" were often seen as "temporal signs" of God’s favor under the Law (Deuteronomy 28:1–14) [409, 934, 950, 1313, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** this by showing that the "true church" is an “assembly of the citizens of heaven” whose "inheritance is incorruptible," for “Jesus answered, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ ” (John 18:36; 1 Peter 1:4) [13, 26, 142, 213, 830, 888, 1313, 1426, 1529, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: God’s Sovereignty Over Economic Divergence**

**Verse**
“ ‘The LORD makes poor and makes rich; He brings low and lifts up. He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the beggar from the ash heap, to set them among princes and make them inherit the throne of glory’ ” (1 Samuel 2:7–8). [940, 1015, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that God “harnesses the deeds of the wicked” and the "choices" of men to "positively ordain whatsoever comes to pass" [1429, 1495, 1496, 1497, 1567, Conversation History]. While "market highs" may coexist with "financial precarity," this is not outside the “sovereign plan” of the King who “raises up kings, then pulls them from their thrones,” for “the silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, says the LORD of hosts” (Haggai 2:8) [15, 318, 926, 1143, 1532, 1720, Conversation History]. Scripture handles the tension between the "rich man" and "Lazarus" by showing that "the rich man... was buried" while "the beggar was carried by angels," proving that God "dispenses as He will" (Luke 16:19–22; Job 11:10) [331, 332, 337, 338, 993, Conversation History]. This reveals that "nothing thwarts any aspect of His plan," even when "unrighteous deception" allows the "greedy" to "exploit for profit" (2 Thessalonians 2:10; 2 Peter 2:3) [5, 11, 21, 563, 1111, 1408, 1484, 1515, 1572, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “trade in your worry for trust,” recognizing that “the LORD has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all” (Psalm 103:19) [15, 94, 201, 1143, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. Do "not be afraid when one becomes rich," for "He who began a good work in you will complete it," and your "daily bread" is a "divine blessing" from a "loving Father" (Psalm 49:16; Philippians 1:6; Matthew 6:11) [5, 51, 53, 55, 58, 829, 1040, 1408, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Ritual vs. Reality**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, "man-made representations" of God were "incinerated" because they attempted to "caricature" Him [237, 315, 1133, 1344, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our view of status, revealing that "God shows no partiality" and "makes no distinction" between "rich and poor," for we are all "heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ" (Acts 10:34; Galatians 3:28; Romans 8:17) [248, 249, 1159, 1167, 1210, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: The Danger of Common Grace vs. Saving Faith**

**Verse**
“ ‘For the sun rises on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust’ ” (Matthew 5:45). [65, 1143, 1160, 1161, 1381, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture teaches that "temporal blessings" and "physical blessings" are part of God’s "common grace" to all "mankind," and it is a "great and common danger" to "confuse human success with divine blessing" [1, 65, 1114, 1143, 1381, Conversation History]. When a society becomes "prosperous," believers often "behave like practical humanists" and "feel little need for spiritual resources," essentially “establishing their own righteousness” while “ignorant of God’s righteousness” (Romans 10:3) [1, 316, 1448, Conversation History]. The Reformed faith warns that a "profession of faith" joined with a heart that is "enthralled with this life" is a "spirit of fraud," for "if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him" (1 John 2:15) [12, 185, 326, 356, 893, 1502, 1605, 1624, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Never become so involved in this world” that you treat the “unfailing Word” as a "platform for your own ego," for “your life is not your own” but is “hid with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3; 1 Corinthians 6:19) [11, 12, 51, 101, 130, 212, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1623, 1670, Conversation History]. You must “discipline your mind” to “hold fast and not let go,” knowing that “the Word of our God stands forever” while "riches... vanish—like smoke they vanish away" (Isaiah 40:8; Psalm 102:3) [10, 11, 32, 116, 121, 1306, 1406, 1684, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Continuity of the Decree**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, "testifying in a dispute" required strict "safeguards" to establish "justice for all" (Deuteronomy 17:6) [330, 367, 1072, 1230, 1317, 1365, 1473, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our "victory," teaching that the “church militant” conquers not through “carnal weaponry” or "political maneuvering and lobbying," but “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11) [13, 16, 21, 32, 92, 1113, 1313, 1402, 1491, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The True Flourishing of the Holy Spirit Temple**

**Verse**
“ ‘Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? For you were bought at a price; therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s’ ” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). [11, 12, 101, 238, 264, 833, 1059, 1138, 1202, 1243, 1262, 1406, 1670, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition—echoed by **Paul Washer** and **Voddie Baucham**—teaches that the "true church" is a "spiritual house" built of "living stones," and flourishing is measured by "spiritual maturity" and "Christlikeness" [17, 402, 749, 751, 889, 1219, 1251, 1253, 1313, 1426, Conversation History]. When you "accept humbly whatever God brings" into your life, you acting as a "vessel for honor" who "adorns the doctrine of God" in the midst of "scarcity" (Titus 2:10; 2 Timothy 2:21) [33, 101, 139, 1131, 1143, 1144, 1195, 1406, 1450, 1502, Conversation History]. The "record of history" reveals that "godliness with contentment is great gain," for “the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (1 Timothy 6:6; Psalm 111:10) [13, 1153, 1323, 1406, 1416, 1503, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “perfect justice will come” and He will “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:10) [14, 24, 94, 109, 201, 470, 816, 822, 948, 1315, 1408, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. Find “repose of the soul” in Christ’s “finished work,” recognizing that “death is but a harmless shadow for the sheep of the Good Shepherd” (John 19:30; John 10:11; Psalm 23:4) [13, 24, 142, 172, 198, 844, 1016, 1313, 1426, 1445, 1646, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 147, 176, 211, 222, 285, 300, 313, 332, 361, 405, 413, 414, 444, 453, 591, 1138, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

We obviously do not realize that we are talking about the ever blessed, eternal, and absolute, almighty God. There is a sense in which we should take our shoes off our feet whenever we use the name.1

Some abandon the sower’s task. They decide that throwing seed around is primitive and unsophisticated—and imagine that they can devise a better use for the field. Why not use it to host a music festival, or turn it into a drive-in theater? But the parable is not about enhancing the quality of the seed, improving the skill of the sower, or finding a more elegant use for the farm. It’s all about the condition of the soil. Whether the Word of God bears fruit in the life of a hearer or not depends ultimately on the condition of that person’s heart. The various heart conditions Jesus illustrates cover the whole range of human possibilities.

A single pearl of perfection, size, and beauty could be of immense value. When Jesus said, “Do not … cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6), He was painting an absurd word picture to illustrate the folly of attempting to reason with people who clearly have nothing but contempt for the truth. Who would ever expect the lowest of unclean brute beasts to appreciate something as valuable as pearls? This merchant sought fine pearls to sell because they were a reliable investment; they increased in value as time went by. As is true today, wise investors would diversify: put some money in the ground, some in pearls, some in real estate. The one thing smart investors did not typically do was put everything into one commodity.

Likewise, the Samaritan woman came to the well because she needed water. Not seeking an encounter with Christ, she providentially met Him and went home redeemed. She, the man born blind (John 9), the apostle Matthew (Matt. 9:9), and countless others have unexpectedly stumbled into the kingdom. The merchant, on the other hand, was on a search specifically for valuable pearls. He knew what he was seeking. He wanted something of genuine, lasting value. He is like the Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8, Cornelius in Acts 10, or the Bereans in Acts 17. He represents someone who is knowingly

The same grace that saves us teaches us that “we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present age, looking for the blessed hope and glorious appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:12–13). “For yet a little while, And He who is coming will come and will not tarry” (Heb. 10:37). In the book of Revelation, Christ repeatedly says, “Behold, I am coming quickly!” (Rev. 3:11; 22:7, 12, 20). That is the lesson underscored by this parable. Christ’s return is imminent. That means it could happen at any time. “The Lord is at hand” (Phil. 4:5). “The coming of the Lord is at hand … the Judge is standing at the door!” (James 5:8–9). Nothing stands in the way of our Lord’s immediate return, and we are taught repeatedly in Scripture that we should be ready, expectant, busy, obedient, loyal, fully prepared, like the wise and faithful servant in this parable—“for you do not know what hour your Lord is coming” (Matt. 24:42).

Jesus summed up His teaching on the matter in one clear exhortation in His Sermon on the Mount: “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:19–21). In Luke 16, our Lord tells a parable that both echoes and illustrates that admonition in a very unusual way. It is the story of a lying, cheating, unfaithful servant who is found out and put on notice that he will be fired. He then cunningly uses his master’s wealth to buy friendships that will be useful for cushioning his fall from grace:

This also underscores our duty to use our money to support the ministry of the gospel. Will people be standing on the edge of glory when you arrive, eager to embrace you, because through your investment in gospel ministry and the extension of the kingdom they heard and believed and gained eternal life in Christ? That’s the imagery Jesus’ exhortation evokes. The unjust steward was liberal with his master’s money in an unethical way. His actions, though unjust, nevertheless won him friends and secured his future. Jesus is reminding His disciples that we are stewards too. Unlike the unjust steward, we have our Lord’s explicit permission—nay, we are under express orders—to be generous with the Master’s resources in order to make friends for eternity.

The parable deals with several extreme opposites: torment and comfort; death and life; hell and heaven. The characters are an extravagantly wealthy man and a beggar who lived in extreme poverty; but their fortunes are reversed in the afterlife. Because the focus is on the misery of the man in hell, it is a deeply disturbing story, and yet Jesus had a gracious purpose in telling it to the Pharisees. He was warning them not to follow their own instincts, traditions, and religious convictions. He was urging them to repent.

At least that’s what those who have drunk deeply from the postmodern spirit of our age would have us believe. They insist it is a mistake to subject our Lord’s narratives to serious systematic analysis in search of a precise interpretation, because to do that is to miss the real purpose of the stories. Instead, we’re told, it’s better to enjoy and admire and adapt Jesus’ stories in whatever way makes them most meaningful to us. According to this way of thinking, since stories are inherently subjective, we should be less concerned with asking what the parables mean—and more concerned with finding ways of making the stories of the Bible our own.*

Providence is God's continuous involvement with His creation whereby He preserves and governs all His creations from the greatest to the least so that in accord with His perfect will and design, He sovereignly orders everything He has made to accomplish everything He intends for His own glory. Now think this through. I just gave you that very straightforward definition which is really no more or less than what we mean when we speak of the sovereignty of God. That's what Ephesians 1:11 means when it says, "God works all things according to the counsel of His own will." And I want to stress this. Regardless of what it may sound like, the doctrine of providence is not held only by Calvinists. In fact, one of the most interesting discussions of providence I know, is from an Arminian theologian named W.B.

If we really believe that not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from God's watchful eye and all-wise plan, and every hair on each head is specifically known by Him, then we don't need to invent phony miracles, or manufacture supernatural phenomena, or imagine that God is speaking fallible words of revelation into our minds in order to justify the conviction that He is personally involved with each one of us. If phony miracles and false prophecies or fabricated signs and wonders somehow make you feel more confident that God is imminent and personally involved in your life, then you are hanging your confidence on a false premise and you need to delve into the study of divine providence. It's a simple basic elementary Christian truth. Paul taught it to the pagan philosophers on Mars Hill. He is not far from each one of us, for in Him we live, and move, and exist.
